chapter: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
title: Hanging out with Fats; Dizzy at the Savoy; Fats with Tadd Dameron
summary: They go to heckle Dizzy's big band at the Savoy; McGhee thinks Fats sounded at home with Dameron and replaced Dizzy with Eckstine.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Did you used to hang out together and go play after the gig?
Oh yeah. We would go to catch Dizzy. We said, 'Let's go hang up Dizzy.'
That was the Savoy Ballroom. We used to say, 'Let's go hang up Dizzy.'
Who was Dizzy playing with then? Lucky Millinder?
No, Dizzy had his band. Dizzy had his big band up there.
This is '45, when he had the first big band?

Yeah, the big band. Yeah, Dizzy was poppin' them, too, but I mean, he always turned it around with something. But we'd go heckle him just for the hell of it, just to egg him on. 'All right, play something, motherfucker,' you know. Not that we hated him or anything. We were just egging him on, to make him play something. That's what we were doing with him then.
Fats sounded beautiful, I thought, with Tadd Dameron. He played with him so beautiful, I thought. I said, 'Well,

gee, that's one group, shit, that he's with that he really feels at home." But I was glad to see him get out of Andy's band, because Andy's band wasn't for him. And Andy didn't never know when a guy was playing good or not. He was nice, but he just didn't know anything about...
Well, I guess then Fats took Dizzy's place with Billy Eckstine.
With Billy Eckstine, yeah. Because Fats was somethin' else, man.
I guess that's when people started to hear about him more, because he was featured on a couple of records...
Yeah. He was doing everything that he could possibly do as far as playing the trumpet was concerned. And he deserved to be recognized. He deserved that at that time.
Well, we'll get into more about that, and then the records you made after this...
